title: The Statistic Nobody Measured
subtitle: Change models and the evidence behind them
summary: A narrated, interactive version of Lesson 2 of Week 12. It covers the same objectives — the evidence behind the 70 per cent failure claim, Kotter’s eight steps and the three-step model as practitioner heuristics, readiness as commitment and efficacy, and resistance as information — and leads into the same comprehension check.

visual.title: The statistic nobody measured
visual.sub: Change models and the evidence behind them

cues.text: Open almost any change-management presentation, and somewhere near the start you will meet the same number.
About seventy percent of organizational change initiatives fail.
It is a useful number. It makes change sound hard, it justifies specialists, and it creates urgency. Today we ask a simple question: where did it come from?

lines: Failure out of what? Defined how? Measured when?
visual.sub: Before you trust a rate, ask for its denominator.

cues.text: Think about what someone would have had to measure to know this.
A denominator: seventy percent of which initiatives? A definition of failure. And a point in time when failure was judged.
A researcher named Mark Hughes went looking for exactly that. He traced the figure through five frequently cited published sources.
What do you think he found?

checkpoint.prompt: Mark Hughes traced the 70 per cent change-failure figure through five frequently cited sources. What did he conclude?

options.text: The figure is well supported by a large multi-company study.
The true rate is lower, closer to 50 per cent.
There is no valid and reliable empirical evidence for the figure.
The figure is accurate, but only for small firms.

feedback.a: No. Hughes found no such study behind the figure; some sources gave it without describing how it was obtained.
feedback.b: Hughes did not replace the number with another one. His point is that nobody has measured a general rate at all.
feedback.c: Right. The narrative is widespread, but Hughes found no valid and reliable empirical evidence behind it.
feedback.d: Nothing in the sources supports a firm-size version either. Some concerned narrower programs such as business-process reengineering.

cards.title: Implementation
cards.fail: Says nothing about the idea itself

cards.title: Effectiveness
cards.q: Carried out, but no intended results
cards.fail: The design may be the problem

cards.title: Net cost
cards.q: Goals met, at too high a price

cues.text: Hughes concluded that, although the seventy percent story is everywhere, there is no valid and reliable empirical evidence for it.
Some of the sources concerned narrower programs, such as business-process reengineering. Others presented the figure without describing how it was obtained.
Part of the problem is that failure is rarely defined. Consider four meanings.
An implementation failure: the change was never carried out as designed.
An effectiveness failure: it was carried out, but did not produce the intended results.
A sustainability failure: results appeared, then faded.
Or the change met its goals, at a cost in trust, turnover or side effects that outweighed them.
And there are measurement problems too. Initiatives are not registered in advance. Their goals shift. Leaders tend to recall success, and consultants hired after trouble tend to see failure.
Hughes also suggests that repeating the figure may itself shape how change is managed and justified. A number nobody measured can still steer budgets and tactics.
Implementation science takes a slower route: prospective studies that define outcomes in advance and measure them at every site. Less quotable, far more useful.

None of this means change usually succeeds. It means nobody knows the base rate. The better question is conditional: among initiatives like this one, in settings like ours, what predicted the outcome?

left.title: Unfreeze – change – refreeze
points: Familiar form took shape after his death in 1947
His actual work was more iterative

cues.text: If the statistic is folklore, what about the models built on top of it?
The most famous is a three-step sequence: unfreeze, change, refreeze. It is usually credited to the social psychologist Kurt Lewin.
Stephen Cummings, Todd Bridgman and Kenneth Brown compared Lewin’s own writings with later presentations. They argue he never developed such a model.
Its familiar form took shape after his death in nineteen forty-seven. His actual work on group dynamics and action research was richer and more iterative.
The second is John Kotter’s eight steps, published in nineteen ninety-five as eight errors he had observed in transformation efforts.
It is drawn from his consulting experience. A synthesis, not a tested theory.
Both remain popular for good reasons. They are memorable, and they point at real problems.

left.title: Useful reminders
points: Explain why the status quo is costly

right.title: Watch out for
points: Easy wins that dodge the root cause

cues.text: So how should you use Kotter’s list? As a practitioner checklist for a planning conversation.
Read it as reminders. Explain why the status quo is costly. Secure people with authority and credibility. Show early progress. Keep going after the first wins.
And read each step with its shadow. Urgency can become a manufactured crisis that erodes trust when exposed. A guiding coalition can be senior allies with no credibility on the frontline.
Short-term wins can be easy wins that avoid the root cause. And communicating a vision can slide into confusing message volume with understanding.
The criticism is about status, not usefulness. These models are often presented as established findings, when they are heuristics.

visual.definition: A shared state with two parts: commitment — we want to — and efficacy — we can.
visual.example: Commitment is strongest when people value the change, not merely comply.

cues.text: Here is an idea from implementation science that is more precise, and that you can actually measure.
Bryan Weiner defines organizational readiness for change as a shared psychological state with two parts.
Change commitment is the group’s shared resolve to implement the change. Change efficacy is its shared belief that it can carry it out.
Commitment is strongest when people value the change. It is weaker when they comply because they feel obliged, or feel they have no choice.
Efficacy depends on how people appraise the task, the resources available and the circumstances. And Weiner argues there is no single best way to raise readiness.

visual.title: Commitment by efficacy
cells: Willing but unsure: training, tools, time, practice
Ready: move quickly, keep feedback open
Not ready: clarify the problem, test the design
Capable skeptics: evidence, involvement, address losses

cues.text: Put the two parts on a grid, because the remedies differ.
A group that wants the change but doubts it can do it is willing but unsure. It needs training, tools, time and early practice.
High on both? Ready. Move quickly, keep feedback loops open, and guard against overconfidence.
Low on both? Not ready. Clarify the problem and test the design with the people affected before scaling anything.
And a group that could do it but does not want to? Capable skeptics. Show evidence, involve them in design, and address what they would lose.
Many rollouts fail by applying the commitment remedy, more inspiring communication, to an efficacy problem.
Let’s try it on a case. A hypothetical law firm is introducing software that drafts first versions of routine agreements.

checkpoint.prompt: In the hypothetical law firm, associates can use the drafting software easily but believe it undermines their development. Which response fits their readiness pattern?

options.text: Redesign their training path so automation does not remove learning, and involve them in the design.
An all-hands message on why the firm must move fast.
Nothing: high efficacy means they are ready.

feedback.a: That is the efficacy remedy, and associates already score high on efficacy. Training does little for a group that doesn’t see why the change is worth making.
feedback.b: Right. High efficacy, low commitment: capable skeptics. Address what they would lose — their development — and give them a role in the design.
feedback.c: Urgency messaging does not answer their actual concern, which is about their own development.
feedback.d: Readiness needs both parts. Efficacy without commitment is the capable-skeptic quadrant.

visual.sub: Associates: commitment problem. Paralegals: efficacy problem.

cues.text: The associates are capable skeptics. They need a redesigned training path.
Now suppose the paralegals show the opposite pattern. They want the software, but lack training time. Willing but unsure. They need protected learning time and early practice.
One rollout, two groups, two remedies. A single campaign would have fitted neither.
The same logic applies in a player development department adopting a new assessment protocol. Veteran coaches may be capable skeptics; newer coaches may be willing but unsure.

cards.title: Content
cards.fail: The only type that should change the design

cues.text: Which brings us to resistance. The standard models mostly treat it as an obstacle. Let me suggest treating it as data.
People facing an ambiguous change build an account of what it means for them. Will they be judged by a new metric? Will their expertise still count? Is this a prelude to cuts?
Sometimes resistance is self-interest or habit. Often it contains information the designers lacked: a workflow the system cannot handle, a hidden cost, a promise broken last time.
So classify each objection before you respond. Is it about content: the design is wrong?
About process: people were not consulted or informed?
Or about consequences for the person: status, workload, job security?
Each needs a different answer. And only content objections should change the design.

visual.sub: Heard during the hypothetical law-firm rollout.

cues.text: Back to the law firm. Here is an objection from someone who drafts these agreements every day.

checkpoint.prompt: “The templates can’t handle cross-border clauses.” What type of objection is this, and what is the right response?

options.text: Content — test it, and if true, change the scope of the rollout.
Process — involve drafters in configuration and publish decisions.
Consequence — reassure the person about their role.
Habit — hold firm and repeat the case for change.

feedback.a: Right. It is a claim about the design itself. Test it; if it is true, the objection has just saved the rollout from a real flaw.
feedback.b: Involvement matters, but this objection makes a specific, testable claim about what the templates can do. That is content.
feedback.c: Nothing here is about status or security. Reassurance would ignore what could be a genuine flaw.
feedback.d: Treating a testable design claim as habit throws away exactly the information the designers lacked.

cards.title: Readiness ≠ destiny
cards.fail: Not the same as a wise change

cues.text: Now, a fair challenge to this lecture. Is the staged-model tradition simply wrong?

Not quite. Kotter’s list captures problems many leaders recognize, like weak coalitions and declaring victory too soon. And some scholars defend the practical value of a staged view, whoever first drew it.
The criticisms worth keeping are more specific. Staged models imply a straight line, while real change loops back as designs are tested.
They are written from the leader’s perspective, so the people receiving the change appear mainly as resistance.
They learn from memorable successes and failures, and ignore the many quiet changes that simply worked or faded.
And the limit applies to my own preferred tool too. High readiness can produce effort without results if the change itself is a poor idea. Readiness measures willingness and confidence, not wisdom.

visual.sub: Urgency built on folklore does not.

cues.text: One last scene. Your chief executive wants to open a rollout by announcing that seventy percent of transformations fail, so we must move fast.
Correcting the chief executive in public is costly. Repeating the number risks your credibility with skeptical professionals who may check it.
A better path: offer a stronger opening built on your own evidence, the specific cost of the status quo here, and explain privately why the borrowed statistic is a liability.

cues.text: Let’s bring it together.
The seventy percent figure has no valid and reliable evidential base. Ask for definitions and denominators.
Kotter’s eight steps and the three-step model credited to Lewin are practitioner heuristics. Use them as checklists, not as science.
Readiness has two parts, commitment and efficacy, with different remedies. And resistance is information: classify it as content, process or consequence before you respond.
Next, take the comprehension check below, the same check as the written lesson. Then open the Change Simulator, and read Hughes’s short, sharp audit of the seventy percent claim.
The written lesson keeps the full Kotter table and the methodological notes. Thank you for working through this with me.
